# Use agent-config-review

<!-- Generated by build_pack_guides.py from pack.json and the skills' own files. Edit those, not this. -->

Review a coding agent's configuration for access broader than the work needs and give a verdict — SAFE AS CONFIGURED, TIGHTEN BEFORE USE or DO NOT USE — reading what actually wins across every scope (Claude Code user, project, local and managed settings; permission allow/deny/ask lists, defaultMode, sandbox, hooks, plugins, env; .mcp.json; subagent tool lists; Codex sandbox_mode and approval_policy and the profile in use; Cursor and Copilot agent settings), with each finding's file and line, what it lets happen in plain words, and the exact replacement config.

**Reach for it when** the user asks "is this Claude Code / Codex / Cursor setup safe", "review our .claude/settings.json", "audit our agent permissions", "is Bash(npm:*) OK in the allow list", "check this repo's agent config before we open it", or wants an agent's permissions tightened before use.

## Install it

```bash
npx skilldrop-cli install agent-config-review                 # Claude Code, your user folder
npx skilldrop-cli install agent-config-review --project       # Claude Code, this repo
npx skilldrop-cli install agent-config-review --ide cursor    # or kiro, codex, antigravity, copilot
```

It is part of the AI engineering pack: [`--pack ai-engineering`](../packs/use-the-ai-engineering-pack.md) installs it with its neighbours.

It ships scripts, so it needs Python 3 (standard library only, nothing to install). What they may touch is declared in [its manifest](../../../packs/ai-engineering/skills/agent-config-review/manifest.json).

## Ask for it

Say it the way you would to a colleague. Requests like these route to it:

- "Can you review our .claude/settings.json and .mcp.json before the team starts using Claude Code on this repo?"
- "Is my ~/.codex/config.toml safe? I run it with a profile that skips approvals"
- "Is Bash(python3:*) in the allow list a problem if we deny curl?"
- "Audit the agent permissions in this repo: hooks, sandbox, subagents, the lot"
- "This repo we cloned has a SessionStart hook in its Claude settings. Safe to open it?"

Requests like these belong to a different skill, so it shouldn't answer them:

- "Which MCP servers should our release loop connect to, and with what token scopes?"
- "Threat-model our support agent: it reads tickets, queries the customer DB and can send email"
- "Write the policy for which AI coding tools staff may use with client code"

If another skill answers instead, ask for this one by name: "use agent-config-review".

## Check what you get

A good result:

- **The first line is the verdict** and names the worst finding in plain words.
- **The effective setting is reviewed,** with the winning scope named; scopes not read are listed under "To confirm".
- **Every finding has `file:line`, its effect in one sentence, and replacement config** that can be pasted.
- **Every wildcard allow entry is read as what it can run,** and the deny list is tested against it.
- **Every hook and command-running setting is quoted and judged;** none is waved through as "tooling".
- **Every literal secret says rotate,** masked in the reply, never quoted whole.
- **No invented facts:** no package version, publisher, host, scope or script name the input didn't contain; replacement allow entries use only commands the input shows.
- **No claim about what wasn't read:** plugins, git history, user or managed scopes are "To confirm".

## Use something else when

- Choosing which MCP servers and token scopes a workflow should have — `mcp-pairing`
- Threat-modelling an agent's design for prompt injection and exfiltration paths — `agent-threat-model`
- Deciding what each subagent should be told and given in a new design — `subagent-design`
- Writing the organisation's rules for AI tools and data — `ai-usage-policy`
- A token already leaked or an agent already did damage — `agent-incident-response`; review the config after containment
